P.title: P.blurb
Electricity: From Ohm's law to the fuse board in your hallway.

P.title: el-basics.summary
Electricity: The three quantities behind every circuit, and the one law that ties them together.

P.title: el-basics.q0.q
Electricity: A 9 V battery drives current through a 450 Ω resistor. What is the current?

P.title: el-basics.q0.x
Electricity: I = V ÷ R = 9 ÷ 450 = 0.02 A, which is 20 mA.

P.title: el-basics.q1.q
Electricity: In the water analogy, what plays the role of voltage?

P.title: el-basics.q1.x
Electricity: Voltage is the push, like pressure. Flow is current; pipe narrowness is resistance.

P.title: el-basics.q2.q
Electricity: You double the resistance and keep the voltage the same. The current…

P.title: el-basics.q2.x
Electricity: I = V ÷ R. Twice the R with the same V gives half the current.

P.title: el-basics.q3.q
Electricity: Why do long cable runs need thicker cables?

P.title: el-basics.q3.o1
Electricity: Resistance grows with length, so a bigger cross-section compensates

P.title: el-basics.q3.x
Electricity: R = ρ × L ÷ A: more area offsets more length.

P.title: el-basics.q4.x
Electricity: Off = open loop, on = closed loop.

P.title: el-basics.c0.text
Electricity: A current is a flow of electric charge. In a metal wire it's electrons nudging each other along. Each electron drifts slowly, but the push travels through the wire almost instantly, like water already filling a hose.\n\nBy convention, current is drawn flowing from + to −, the opposite way to the electrons. Every circuit diagram uses this convention.

P.title: el-basics.c1.text
Electricity:
Picture a tank feeding a pipe.
• Voltage is the pressure, set by how high the water stands.
• Current is how much water flows per second.
• Resistance is a narrow section of pipe that limits the flow.

More pressure pushes more flow; a narrower pipe allows less. That's the whole idea behind Ohm's law.

P.title: el-basics.c2.text
Electricity: Voltage (volts, V) equals current (amps, A) times resistance (ohms, Ω). Cover the quantity you want in the triangle and the other two tell you how to get it.

P.title: el-basics.c2.example.0
Electricity: 12 V battery across a 4 Ω heater

P.title: el-basics.c3.text
Electricity: Change the voltage and the resistance. Watch the current and the power the bulb turns into light and heat.

P.title: el-basics.c4.text
Electricity:
Your body is a resistor too. What matters for safety is how much current passes through it, and which way.
Around 1 mA you feel a tingle. Near 10 mA muscles can lock and you may not be able to let go. From roughly 50–100 mA across the chest, the heart can go into fibrillation.

That's why home RCDs trip at 30 mA: well before the dangerous zone.

P.title: el-basics.c5.text
Electricity: In metals, some electrons are free to move, so current flows easily: copper, aluminium, silver. In insulators such as plastic, rubber, glass and dry wood, electrons are held tightly and almost no current flows.\n\nCables combine both: a copper core inside a plastic jacket.

P.title: el-basics.c6.text
Electricity: A wire's resistance grows with its length and shrinks with its cross-section. That's why long cable runs need thicker cables, and why thin extension leads get warm.

P.title: el-basics.c7.text
Electricity: Prefixes keep the numbers manageable. A phone charger supplies about 2 A, a sensor draws a few milliamps, and the national grid carries kilovolts.

P.title: el-basics.c8.text
Electricity: A short circuit is a path with almost no resistance between live and neutral. By Ohm's law, the current becomes enormous, heating cables in a fraction of a second. Fuses and breakers exist to cut it off before a fire starts.

P.title: el-basics.c9.text
Electricity: Current only flows around a complete loop. A switch simply opens the loop (off) or closes it (on). A broken wire, a blown fuse or a loose terminal all open the circuit.

P.title: el-home.summary
Electricity: Series vs parallel, power, and what the breakers in your board actually do.

P.title: el-home.q0.q
Electricity: Why does each socket in a house get the full 230 V?

P.title: el-home.q0.o2
Electricity: Each socket has its own transformer

P.title: el-home.q0.x
Electricity: In parallel, every load sits directly between live and neutral, so each sees the full supply voltage.

P.title: el-home.q1.q
Electricity: A 1150 W heater runs on 230 V. How much current does it draw?

P.title: el-home.q2.o1
Electricity: Current going out on live doesn't all return on neutral

P.title: el-home.q2.x
Electricity: An RCD measures the imbalance between live and neutral. Overcurrent is the breaker's job.

P.title: el-home.q3.q
Electricity: A 1.5 kW oven runs for 4 hours. How much energy is that?

P.title: el-home.q4.q
Electricity: A 6.9 kVA contract allows roughly how much current at 230 V?

P.title: el-home.q5.q
Electricity: 20 W of standby, all year, uses about…

P.title: el-home.c0.text
Electricity: In series, components share a single loop. The same current flows through each and the voltage is split between them. One break stops everything, like old Christmas lights.\n\nIn parallel, each component has its own path to the supply. Each gets the full voltage and can be switched on or off independently.

P.title: el-home.c1.title
Electricity: Your house is wired in parallel

P.title: el-home.c1.text
Electricity: Every socket and light hangs between the live (L) and neutral (N) conductors. That's why each appliance gets the full 230 V, and why switching off the kettle doesn't turn off the fridge.\n\nThe more you plug in, the more total current flows in the live wire. That total is what breakers watch.

P.title: el-home.c2.text
Electricity: Power (watts) is how fast energy is used. Multiply the voltage by the current. Rearranged, I = P ÷ V tells you how much current an appliance draws.

P.title: el-home.c3.text
Electricity: A breaker (MCB) protects the cable. If too much current flows, the wire would overheat, so it trips. A 16 A breaker on a socket circuit is typical.\n\nAn RCD protects people. It compares the current going out on live with the current coming back on neutral. If about 30 mA is missing, it has leaked somewhere, maybe through a person, and it trips in a fraction of a second.

P.title: el-home.c4.text
Electricity: You pay for energy, not power. Energy = power × time, measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh). One kWh is 1 kW running for one hour.

P.title: el-home.c5.text
Electricity: In Portugal and much of Europe, homes are split into circuits, each with its own breaker: lighting, general sockets, kitchen, and big appliances like the oven or water heater.

P.title: el-home.c6.text
Electricity: Many devices draw power even when "off": TV, router, chargers, coffee machine. Each may use only a few watts, but running all year, it adds up.

P.title: el-home.c7.text
Electricity: In Portugal you contract a maximum power with your supplier, such as 6.9 kVA. If you switch on too many appliances at once, the main breaker (ICP) trips. Higher contracted power means a higher fixed daily charge.

P.title: el-home.c8.text
Electricity: Contracted power 6.9 kVA ≈ 30 A at 230 V. Oven (2 kW), kettle (2.2 kW) and washing machine heating (2 kW) together make 6.2 kW: close to the limit. Add a 2 kW heater and the main breaker trips.

P.title: el-home.c9.text
Electricity: Portugal uses the Schuko-type socket (type F) with side earth clips. The UK uses type G with three rectangular pins and a fuse inside the plug.

P.title: el-acdc.summary
Electricity: Why the socket alternates and the battery doesn't.

P.title: el-acdc.q0.o1
Electricity: The current reverses direction 50 times a second (50 cycles)

P.title: el-acdc.q1.q
Electricity: Why did AC win for power grids?

P.title: el-acdc.q1.o1
Electricity: Transformers can step its voltage up and down easily

P.title: el-acdc.q2.x
Electricity: Panels make DC; the house uses AC.

P.title: el-acdc.c0.text
Electricity: In DC, current flows in one direction at a constant voltage. Batteries, solar panels and USB chargers supply DC, and every electronic circuit runs on it internally.

P.title: el-acdc.c1.text
Electricity: In AC, the voltage swings positive and negative in a smooth wave, reversing direction many times a second. European mains reverses 50 times a second: 50 hertz.

P.title: el-acdc.c2.text
Electricity: Mains is quoted as 230 V, but that's the RMS value: the DC voltage that would deliver the same heating power. The actual peaks reach about 325 V.

P.title: el-acdc.c3.text
Electricity: In the 1880s Edison promoted DC; Westinghouse and Tesla backed AC. AC won for power grids because transformers could easily step its voltage up for long-distance transmission and down for homes.

P.title: el-acdc.c3.viz.events.0.l
Electricity: Edison's DC station in New York

P.title: el-acdc.c3.viz.events.2.l
Electricity: AC lights the Chicago World's Fair

P.title: el-acdc.c4.text
Electricity: Power losses in cables depend on the square of the current. Transformers raise the voltage so the same power flows with far less current, and losses drop dramatically. Transformers only work with AC.

P.title: el-acdc.c5.text
Electricity: Your laptop charger turns AC into DC (a rectifier plus regulator). A solar inverter does the opposite, turning DC from panels into AC for the house.

P.title: el-acdc.c6.text
Electricity: Modern electronics can convert DC voltages efficiently, so very long undersea and overland links now use high-voltage DC (HVDC). Data centres and EVs are also largely DC inside.

P.title: el-acdc.c7.text
Electricity: Every generator on a grid spins in sync. If demand suddenly exceeds supply, the frequency drops slightly below 50 Hz, and operators must add power within seconds to bring it back.

P.title: el-acdc.c8.text
Electricity: Generators produce a sine wave naturally because their coils rotate through a magnetic field. One full turn of a two-pole generator makes one cycle; at 3,000 rpm that's 50 cycles a second.

P.title: el-acdc.c9.text
Electricity: Most of the world uses 220–240 V at 50 Hz. North America uses 120 V at 60 Hz, and Japan is split: 50 Hz in the east, 60 Hz in the west.

P.title: el-magnet.summary
Electricity: How current makes magnetic fields and vice versa.

P.title: el-magnet.q0.o1
Electricity: An electric current creates a magnetic field

P.title: el-magnet.q0.x
Electricity: A compass needle moved near a current.

P.title: el-magnet.q1.q
Electricity: Why doesn't an aluminium pan work on an induction hob?

P.title: el-magnet.q1.o1
Electricity: It isn't magnetic enough for the field to heat it efficiently

P.title: el-magnet.q2.q
Electricity: A relay lets a small current…

P.title: el-magnet.q2.x
Electricity: The coil pulls a separate contact closed.

P.title: el-magnet.c0.text
Electricity: A magnet has a north and a south pole. Opposite poles attract; like poles repel. The invisible region where it acts is its magnetic field, which iron filings make visible as curved lines.

P.title: el-magnet.c1.text
Electricity: Earth's molten iron core creates a magnetic field. A compass needle is a tiny magnet that lines up with it. Magnetic north drifts slowly and isn't exactly the geographic North Pole.

P.title: el-magnet.c1.viz.steps.0
Electricity: Molten iron flows in the core

P.title: el-magnet.c2.text
Electricity: In 1820 Ørsted noticed a compass needle twitch near a wire carrying current. Every current creates a magnetic field circling around it. This links electricity and magnetism.

P.title: el-magnet.c3.text
Electricity: Wind wire into a coil and the fields add up. Put an iron core inside and the field becomes much stronger. Switch off the current and the magnet switches off too.

P.title: el-magnet.c4.text
Electricity: Relays, door locks, loudspeakers, MRI scanners, scrapyard cranes and the contactors in your fuse board all use electromagnets.

P.title: el-magnet.c5.text
Electricity: A relay uses a small current through a coil to pull a switch closed. That lets a 3.3 V microcontroller safely switch a 230 V heater on and off.

P.title: el-magnet.c6.text
Electricity: Faraday discovered the reverse in 1831: a changing magnetic field pushes current through a nearby wire. Move a magnet in and out of a coil and current flows. This is how generators and transformers work.

P.title: el-magnet.c7.text
Electricity: An induction hob runs high-frequency AC through a coil under the glass. The changing field induces currents directly in the iron pan, which heats up. The glass stays relatively cool, and non-magnetic pans don't work.

P.title: el-magnet.c8.text
Electricity: Phone chargers use the same idea: a coil in the pad creates a changing field, and a coil in the phone picks it up. It's convenient but less efficient than a cable, and needs good alignment.

P.title: el-magnet.c9.text
Electricity: Hard drives store bits as tiny regions magnetised one way or the other. Credit-card stripes and old cassette tapes use the same principle.

P.title: el-motors.summary
Electricity: Turning electricity into motion and back again.

P.title: el-motors.q1.q
Electricity: Why do variable speed drives save so much energy on fans?

P.title: el-motors.q1.o1
Electricity: Fan power falls with roughly the cube of speed

P.title: el-motors.q1.x
Electricity: A small speed cut gives a big power cut.

P.title: el-motors.q2.o1
Electricity: Turns the motor into a generator to recharge the battery

P.title: el-motors.c0.text
Electricity: A wire carrying current inside a magnetic field feels a force. Bend the wire into a loop on an axle and the forces on each side push in opposite directions: it turns.

P.title: el-motors.c1.text
Electricity: Small DC motors use a commutator, a split ring that reverses the current every half turn so the coil keeps spinning the same way. Brushes rub on it, which causes wear.

P.title: el-motors.c2.text
Electricity: A generator is a motor in reverse: spin a coil in a magnetic field (or a magnet inside coils) and a voltage is induced. Turbines driven by steam, water or wind turn generators to make almost all our electricity.

P.title: el-motors.c3.text
Electricity: Most industrial motors, pumps and fans are AC induction motors. The stator creates a rotating magnetic field; it induces currents in the rotor, which chases the field around. Simple, tough, no brushes.

P.title: el-motors.c4.title
Electricity: Motors use a lot of electricity

P.title: el-motors.c4.text
Electricity: Electric motors account for roughly 40–45% of global electricity use, according to the IEA, mostly in industry: pumps, compressors and fans. More efficient motors and speed control save huge amounts of energy.

P.title: el-motors.c4.viz.items.0.l
Electricity: of world electricity runs motors (IEA estimate)

P.title: el-motors.c5.text
Electricity: A variable frequency drive (VFD) changes the frequency fed to an AC motor to control its speed. Since fan and pump power falls steeply with speed, running at 80% speed can use only about half the power.

P.title: el-motors.c6.text
Electricity: Electric cars use permanent-magnet or induction motors, often over 90% efficient, versus roughly 20–35% for petrol engines. They deliver full torque from standstill.

P.title: el-motors.c7.text
Electricity: When an EV slows down, its motor runs as a generator, turning motion back into electricity to recharge the battery. That's why one-pedal driving extends range in city traffic.

P.title: el-motors.c8.text
Electricity: Stepper motors move in exact steps (3D printers, CNC). Servos use feedback to hold a precise angle (robot arms, RC planes). Both are motion you can control precisely.

P.title: el-motors.c9.text
Electricity: Every motor has a nameplate: rated power (kW), voltage, current, speed (rpm) and efficiency class (IE1 to IE5). It tells you what supply and protection it needs.

P.title: el-grid.summary
Electricity: From power station to your socket.

P.title: el-grid.q0.q
Electricity: Why is electricity transmitted at very high voltage?

P.title: el-grid.q0.o1
Electricity: Less current is needed, so cable losses are much lower

P.title: el-grid.q1.o1
Electricity: A changing magnetic field induces a voltage in the second coil

P.title: el-grid.q2.o1
Electricity: Pumps water uphill when power is cheap and generates later

P.title: el-grid.c0.text
Electricity: Electricity is generated in power stations and wind or solar farms, carried long distances on high-voltage transmission lines, then distributed at lower voltages to towns and homes.

P.title: el-grid.c1.text
Electricity: A transformer has two coils around an iron core. AC in the first coil creates a changing field that induces voltage in the second. The ratio of turns sets the ratio of voltages.

P.title: el-grid.c2.text
Electricity: Cable losses equal I² × R. Doubling the voltage halves the current for the same power, cutting losses to a quarter.

P.title: el-grid.c3.text
Electricity: Electricity is hard to store in bulk, so supply must match demand every second. Grid operators forecast demand and dispatch power plants, imports, storage and demand response to keep the balance.

P.title: el-grid.c4.text
Electricity: Demand is low at night, rises in the morning and peaks in the evening when people cook and heat homes. Solar output peaks at midday, which is shifting when power is cheapest.

P.title: el-grid.c5.text
Electricity: Renewables (hydro, wind, solar and biomass) supply the majority of Portugal's electricity in a typical year, roughly 60–70% in recent years depending on rainfall and wind. In 2016, the country ran four days straight on renewables alone.

P.title: el-grid.c6.text
Electricity: Portugal's grid is linked to Spain's, and Spain's to France. Interconnections let countries share surplus wind or solar, but the Iberian Peninsula's links to the rest of Europe are relatively limited.

P.title: el-grid.c7.text
Electricity: On 28 April 2025, a sudden loss of generation triggered a cascade that blacked out almost all of mainland Spain and Portugal for many hours. Restoring a grid from zero ("black start") is slow and delicate.

P.title: el-grid.c8.text
Electricity: Pumped hydro stores energy by pumping water uphill when power is cheap and releasing it through turbines when needed. Large batteries now respond in milliseconds to stabilise frequency.

P.title: el-grid.c9.text
Electricity: Smart meters, sensors and automation let the grid see where power flows in real time, integrate rooftop solar and EVs, and reroute around faults automatically.

P.title: el-batteries.summary
Electricity: Chemistry, capacity and how to make them last.

P.title: el-batteries.q0.q
Electricity: A 12 V, 50 Ah battery stores about…

P.title: el-batteries.q2.q
Electricity: What speeds up battery ageing the most?

P.title: el-batteries.q2.x
Electricity: Heat and high states of charge add stress.

P.title: el-batteries.c0.text
Electricity: A battery has two electrodes separated by an electrolyte. A chemical reaction pushes electrons out of one electrode, through your circuit, and back into the other. Recharging reverses the reaction.

P.title: el-batteries.c1.text
Electricity: Amp-hours (Ah) say how much charge a battery holds. Multiply by voltage to get energy in watt-hours (Wh), which is what really matters for comparing batteries.

P.title: el-batteries.c2.text
Electricity: Lead-acid is cheap and heavy (car starter batteries). Lithium-ion packs far more energy per kilo (phones, laptops, EVs). LFP, a lithium iron phosphate variant, trades a little energy density for safety and long life.

P.title: el-batteries.c3.text
Electricity: The C-rate compares charge or discharge current with capacity. 1C fully charges or empties a battery in about an hour; 0.5C in two hours; 3C in 20 minutes. High C-rates create heat and wear.

P.title: el-batteries.c4.text
Electricity: Lithium batteries last longer if kept away from 0% and 100% for long periods. Many EVs recommend charging to 80% for daily use and 100% only before long trips.

P.title: el-batteries.c5.text
Electricity: Each cycle causes tiny chemical changes that slowly reduce capacity. Heat speeds this up a lot. High charge levels and very fast charging add stress too.

P.title: el-batteries.c6.text
Electricity: LFP cells can often manage several thousand full cycles before falling to 80% capacity, which is why they're popular for home storage. Typical NMC cells manage fewer, but store more energy per kilo.

P.title: el-batteries.c7.text
Electricity: A BMS watches every cell's voltage and temperature, balances them, limits current and disconnects the pack if anything goes wrong. Lithium packs must never be used without one.

P.title: el-batteries.c8.text
Electricity: If a lithium cell is damaged, overcharged or overheated, it can start a self-heating reaction that spreads to neighbouring cells. Such fires are hard to extinguish and can reignite.

P.title: el-batteries.c9.text
Electricity: Cells in series add voltage; cells in parallel add capacity. An EV pack might combine about 100 groups in series to reach roughly 400 V.

P.title: el-solar.summary
Electricity: How panels turn sunlight into electricity.

P.title: el-solar.q0.o1
Electricity: Watt-peak, output under standard test conditions

P.title: el-solar.q1.q
Electricity: Which direction should panels face in Portugal for maximum yearly energy?

P.title: el-solar.q1.x
Electricity: The sun crosses the southern sky.

P.title: el-solar.q2.q
Electricity: Why do hot panels produce less?

P.title: el-solar.q2.o1
Electricity: Silicon cells lose efficiency as temperature rises

P.title: el-solar.c0.text
Electricity: A solar cell is a thin slice of silicon with two differently treated layers. Light knocks electrons loose, and the junction between the layers pushes them in one direction: a DC current.

P.title: el-solar.c1.text
Electricity: A cell makes about 0.5–0.6 V. Dozens of cells in series make a panel; several panels in series make a string with a few hundred volts, feeding an inverter.

P.title: el-solar.c2.text
Electricity: Panels are rated in watt-peak (Wp): output under standard test conditions of 1,000 W/m² of sunlight at 25 °C. Real output is usually lower because of heat, angle and dust.

P.title: el-solar.c3.text
Electricity: In Portugal, each kWp of well-oriented panels typically produces around 1,400–1,700 kWh a year, among the best in Europe.

P.title: el-solar.c4.text
Electricity: In Portugal, panels facing south at around 30–35° give the most energy over a year. East–west layouts produce less in total but spread production across the day.

P.title: el-solar.c5.text
Electricity: A small shadow on one cell can cut a whole string's output, because cells in series carry the same current. Bypass diodes and optimisers limit the damage.

P.title: el-solar.c6.text
Electricity: Silicon cells lose roughly 0.3–0.4% of output per °C above 25 °C. On a hot summer roof the cells can reach 60 °C, losing over 10%.

P.title: el-solar.c7.text
Electricity: Solar power is worth most when you use it as it's produced, because exported power earns less than imported power costs. Run the dishwasher, heat water or charge the car at midday.

P.title: el-solar.c7.viz.items.2
Electricity: Charge the EV in the sun

P.title: el-solar.c7.viz.items.3
Electricity: Add a battery for the evening

P.title: el-solar.c8.text
Electricity: String inverters convert DC from the panels into AC for the home. Hybrid inverters can also charge and discharge a battery. Microinverters sit behind each panel.

P.title: el-solar.c9.text
Electricity: In sunny Portugal, a home system often pays for itself in roughly 5–8 years, depending on price, self-consumption and tariffs. Panels typically carry 25-year performance warranties.

P.title: el-cables.summary
Electricity: Cross-sections, voltage drop and why size matters.

P.title: el-cables.q0.q
Electricity: Which wire colour is protective earth in Europe?

P.title: el-cables.q0.x
Electricity: Brown live, blue neutral, green-yellow earth.

P.title: el-cables.q1.q
Electricity: A 2.5 mm² socket circuit keeps tripping its 16 A breaker. What's right?

P.title: el-cables.q1.o1
Electricity: Find the overload or split the circuit

P.title: el-cables.q2.q
Electricity: Why must a reel extension be unrolled for big loads?

P.title: el-cables.q2.o1
Electricity: Coiled cable can't shed heat and may melt

P.title: el-cables.c0.text
Electricity: Every cable has some resistance, so current heats it (I² × R). Too small a cable for the current overheats, damages its insulation and can start a fire.

P.title: el-cables.c1.text
Electricity: Cable size is the copper area in square millimetres. Bigger area, lower resistance, more current it can safely carry.

P.title: el-cables.c2.text
Electricity: Common practice in Portugal: 1.5 mm² for lighting, 2.5 mm² for sockets, 4 mm² for ovens or water heaters, 6 mm² for an EV charger or big heat pump. Always check the installation rules and the installer's calculation.

P.title: el-cables.c3.text
Electricity: The breaker must be rated so the cable can never carry more than it safely can. Swapping a 16 A breaker for a 25 A one "because it keeps tripping" removes the protection.

P.title: el-cables.c3.viz.items.1.r
Electricity: rewire with thicker cable if needed

P.title: el-cables.c4.text
Electricity: Long cables lose voltage along the way. Rules usually limit the drop to a few percent. Single-phase drop is roughly twice the length times current times resistance per metre.

P.title: el-cables.c5.text
Electricity: A cable buried in insulation or bundled with others can't shed heat, so it carries less current safely than one in open air.

P.title: el-cables.c6.text
Electricity: In Europe: brown is live (phase), blue is neutral, green-and-yellow is protective earth. Older Portuguese installations may use different colours, so never trust colours alone.

P.title: el-cables.c7.text
Electricity: Fixed wiring uses solid or stranded rigid conductors. Appliance leads and extension cords use flexible multi-strand cable that survives bending.

P.title: el-cables.c8.text
Electricity: A reel extension must be fully unrolled for high loads, otherwise the coiled cable traps heat and can melt. Never daisy-chain multi-plug adapters for heaters or kettles.

P.title: el-cables.c8.viz.items.1
Electricity: Check the max watts on the label

P.title: el-cables.c9.text
Electricity: Aluminium conducts about 60% as well as copper, so it needs a bigger cross-section, but it's lighter and cheaper. Overhead power lines use aluminium; home wiring uses copper.

P.title: el-earthing.summary
Electricity: Breakers, RCDs, earth and surge protection.

P.title: el-earthing.q0.q
Electricity: Which RCD detects smooth DC leakage, as needed for many EV chargers?

P.title: el-earthing.q1.q
Electricity: Why use RCBOs on each circuit?

P.title: el-earthing.q1.o1
Electricity: A fault only trips that circuit

P.title: el-earthing.q2.q
Electricity: What does an SPD protect against?

P.title: el-earthing.q2.o1
Electricity: Short voltage spikes from lightning or switching

P.title: el-earthing.c0.text
Electricity: Metal cases of appliances are connected to earth. If a live wire touches the case, current rushes to earth instead of through you, and a protective device trips.

P.title: el-earthing.c1.text
Electricity: In many homes the earth connection ends at a copper rod or ring buried in the ground. Its resistance must be low enough for protective devices to work, and it should be tested periodically.

P.title: el-earthing.c2.text
Electricity: An MCB trips two ways: a bimetallic strip for slow overloads (heat), and an electromagnet for short circuits (instant). The letter (B, C, D) sets how sensitive it is to inrush currents.

P.title: el-earthing.c3.text
Electricity: Type B trips magnetically at 3–5× its rating, good for homes. Type C at 5–10×, for motors and lighting with big inrush. Type D at 10–20×, for heavy industrial motors.

P.title: el-earthing.c3.viz.unit
Electricity: magnetic trip (× rated current, upper bound)

P.title: el-earthing.c4.text
Electricity: Type AC detects only AC leakage. Type A also detects pulsing DC from electronics. Type B detects smooth DC too, often required for EV chargers and some solar inverters (or Type A with a DC-detection device).

P.title: el-earthing.c4.viz.items.1
Electricity: Type A: AC and pulsing DC

P.title: el-earthing.c5.text
Electricity: An RCBO combines an MCB and an RCD in one device, so a fault on one circuit only trips that circuit instead of the whole house.

P.title: el-earthing.c6.text
Electricity: Lightning and grid switching can cause voltage spikes of thousands of volts for microseconds. A surge protection device (SPD) in the fuse board diverts them to earth, protecting electronics.

P.title: el-earthing.c7.text
Electricity: RCDs have a test button that simulates a leak. Pressing it every few months checks that the mechanism isn't stuck. If it doesn't trip, call an electrician.

P.title: el-earthing.c8.text
Electricity: Some appliances have no earth wire: they're double insulated, shown by a square inside a square. Two layers of insulation protect you instead of an earth connection.

P.title: el-earthing.c9.text
Electricity: A fuse is a thin wire that melts when too much current flows. It works only once and must be replaced with the same rating. Old Portuguese installations may still have them; modern boards use breakers.

P.title: el-3phase.summary
Electricity: Why industry, big heat pumps and fast chargers use three wires.

P.title: el-3phase.q0.q
Electricity: Voltage between two phases of a European three-phase supply is about…

P.title: el-3phase.q1.q
Electricity: How do you reverse a three-phase motor?

P.title: el-3phase.q1.x
Electricity: Changing the phase order reverses the rotating field.

P.title: el-3phase.q2.q
Electricity: Roughly how much power does 16 A per phase at 400 V give?

P.title: el-3phase.c0.text
Electricity: Three-phase supply has three live conductors, each carrying an AC wave shifted by a third of a cycle (120°). At any moment at least one phase is near its peak, so power flows smoothly.

P.title: el-3phase.c1.text
Electricity: Between any phase and neutral you get 230 V; between two phases you get 400 V. Homes with three-phase supply still use 230 V for normal sockets.

P.title: el-3phase.c2.text
Electricity: Three-phase carries about three times the power of a single phase with the same current per wire.

P.title: el-3phase.c2.example.0
Electricity: 16 A per phase at 400 V, cos φ = 1

P.title: el-3phase.c3.text
Electricity: Three-phase motors are simpler, smaller and self-starting, and transmission needs less copper for the same power. Nearly all generation, transmission and industrial loads are three-phase.

P.title: el-3phase.c4.text
Electricity: Larger homes in Portugal may have three-phase supply. It allows more contracted power, 11 kW or 22 kW EV charging, and big heat pumps, while circuits are spread across phases.

P.title: el-3phase.c5.text
Electricity: Loads should be spread evenly across the three phases. If one phase carries most of the load, it may trip while the others are lightly used, and the neutral carries extra current.

P.title: el-3phase.c6.text
Electricity: The order in which phases peak (L1, L2, L3) sets the direction a three-phase motor turns. Swap any two phases and the motor runs backwards: a classic commissioning check.

P.title: el-3phase.c7.text
Electricity: Three-phase windings can be connected in star (Y), with a shared neutral point, or delta (Δ), in a triangle. Large motors often start in star to limit current, then switch to delta.

P.title: el-3phase.c8.text
Electricity: From the generator to the distribution transformer on your street, power travels as three-phase. Each house on a single-phase supply is connected to one of the three phases.

P.title: el-3phase.c8.viz.steps.3
Electricity: Houses spread across L1, L2, L3

P.title: el-3phase.c9.text
Electricity: A three-phase board has three-pole or four-pole breakers and often a red CEE socket (5-pin) for machines. Three-phase meters show three readings.

P.title: el-3phase.c9.viz.items.2
Electricity: Three voltage readings on the meter

P.title: el-3phase.c9.viz.items.3
Electricity: Brown, black and grey phase wires

P.title: el-pf.summary
Electricity: Real power, reactive power and why the grid cares.

P.title: el-pf.q0.q
Electricity: A load draws 1,000 VA with a power factor of 0.8. Its real power is…

P.title: el-pf.q1.q
Electricity: What corrects a lagging power factor in a factory?

P.title: el-pf.q2.q
Electricity: Which device has a power factor of about 1?

P.title: el-pf.q2.x
Electricity: Pure resistance keeps current in step with voltage.

P.title: el-pf.c0.text
Electricity: With some loads, current and voltage don't peak at the same time. Then volts × amps (apparent power, in VA) is larger than the useful power that actually does work (real power, in W).

P.title: el-pf.c1.text
Electricity: Picture a glass of beer: the liquid is real power that quenches thirst; the foam is reactive power that takes space but does no work. The whole glass is apparent power.

P.title: el-pf.c2.text
Electricity: Motors, transformers and fluorescent ballasts store energy in magnetic fields each cycle and give it back, so their current lags the voltage. Cheap electronics distort the current wave.

P.title: el-pf.c3.text
Electricity: A low power factor means more current for the same useful work: bigger cables, more losses, larger transformers. Utilities charge industrial customers for reactive energy.

P.title: el-pf.c4.text
Electricity: Capacitors draw current that leads the voltage, cancelling a motor's lagging current. Factories install capacitor banks to bring the power factor close to 1.

P.title: el-pf.c5.text
Electricity: Real power in watts (W), reactive power in volt-amperes reactive (var), apparent power in volt-amperes (VA). UPS units and generators are rated in VA because their wiring must handle the full current.

P.title: el-pf.c6.text
Electricity: Real and reactive power are at right angles, so apparent power is the hypotenuse: VA² = W² + var². The angle between them is φ.

P.title: el-pf.c7.text
Electricity: Households in Portugal pay for active energy (kWh) only; reactive energy charges apply to larger commercial and industrial customers. Your contracted power, though, is in kVA.

P.title: el-pf.c8.text
Electricity: Resistive loads like kettles and heaters have a power factor of 1. Motors run around 0.8–0.9 at full load and much lower when lightly loaded.

P.title: el-pf.c9.text
Electricity: Larger electronic power supplies, including laptop and EV chargers, contain power factor correction circuits that make the current follow the voltage wave, as required by EU rules.

P.title: el-meter.summary
Electricity: Measuring volts, amps, ohms and continuity safely.

P.title: el-meter.q0.q
Electricity: To measure current, the meter must be…

P.title: el-meter.q0.o1
Electricity: In series, so current flows through it

P.title: el-meter.q1.o1
Electricity: They measure current without breaking the circuit

P.title: el-meter.q1.x
Electricity: They sense the magnetic field around a conductor.

P.title: el-meter.q2.q
Electricity: What must you do before working on a circuit you switched off?

P.title: el-meter.q2.o1
Electricity: Prove it dead with a tester you've checked on a live source

P.title: el-meter.q2.x
Electricity: Prove dead, and prove the tester works.

P.title: el-meter.c0.text
Electricity: A multimeter measures voltage, current and resistance, and usually continuity, diodes and sometimes capacitance and temperature. A rotary dial chooses the function and range.

P.title: el-meter.c1.text
Electricity: Set the dial to V (AC ~ or DC ⎓), put the probes across the two points, in parallel. The meter has very high resistance, so it barely disturbs the circuit.

P.title: el-meter.c2.text
Electricity: Current must flow through the meter, in series: break the circuit and insert the meter. Move the red lead to the A or mA socket. Forgetting to move it back is the classic way to blow the meter's fuse.

P.title: el-meter.c2.viz.r.items.2
Electricity: red lead in A or mA

P.title: el-meter.c3.text
Electricity: Measure resistance only on unpowered circuits. Continuity mode beeps when the resistance is very low: perfect for finding broken wires or checking which cable is which.

P.title: el-meter.c4.text
Electricity: Meters carry a category rating for where they're safe to use. CAT II covers plugged-in appliances, CAT III the fixed installation and fuse boards, CAT IV the supply origin. Use at least CAT III 600 V on house wiring.

P.title: el-meter.c4.viz.items.0
Electricity: CAT IV: supply origin, meter tails

P.title: el-meter.c4.viz.items.1
Electricity: CAT III: fuse boards, fixed wiring

P.title: el-meter.c5.text
Electricity: A clamp meter measures current without breaking the circuit: you clamp it around a single conductor and it reads the magnetic field. Clamp around the whole cable and live and neutral cancel out.

P.title: el-meter.c6.text
Electricity: Auto-ranging meters pick the range for you. True RMS meters measure non-sinusoidal waveforms (from inverters, LED drivers, VFDs) correctly; cheaper meters can be quite wrong on these.

P.title: el-meter.c7.text
Electricity: To check a socket is live, measure between live and neutral (about 230 V), live and earth (about 230 V) and neutral and earth (near 0 V). Proper socket testers also check earth and RCD.

P.title: el-meter.c8.text
Electricity: Before working on any circuit: isolate it, lock it off, test it's dead with a proven tester, and re-check the tester on a known live source. Never trust a switch or a label alone.

P.title: el-meter.c8.viz.steps.1
Electricity: Test tester on a live source

P.title: el-meter.c9.text
Electricity: Multimeters are great for electronics: battery health (a "12 V" battery should read about 12.6 V when full), sensor outputs, and checking a 3.3 V rail on an ESP32 board.

P.title: el-ev.summary
Electricity: AC, DC, kW and why charging slows down.

P.title: el-ev.q0.q
Electricity: Who converts AC to DC during home AC charging?

P.title: el-ev.q0.x
Electricity: AC charging uses the car's own charger.

P.title: el-ev.q1.q
Electricity: Why does fast charging slow above about 80%?

P.title: el-ev.q1.o1
Electricity: To protect the battery as it fills

P.title: el-ev.q1.x
Electricity: The battery management system tapers the current.

P.title: el-ev.q2.q
Electricity: Adding 40 kWh with an 11 kW charger takes about…

P.title: el-ev.c0.text
Electricity: At home and on most street posts, the car receives AC and converts it to DC with its own on-board charger. The car's charger limits the speed, usually 7–11 kW.

P.title: el-ev.c1.text
Electricity: Fast chargers convert AC to DC in the station and feed the battery directly, bypassing the car's charger. Powers range from 50 kW to 350 kW.

P.title: el-ev.c2.text
Electricity: A normal socket gives about 2.3 kW (10 A at 230 V), slow but fine overnight for short commutes. A single-phase wallbox at 32 A gives about 7.4 kW.

P.title: el-ev.c3.text
Electricity: Divide the energy needed by the charging power, then add some margin for losses and the slower final stage.

P.title: el-ev.c4.text
Electricity: DC charging is fastest at low states of charge and slows down as the battery fills, to protect it. Going from 10% to 80% often takes about as long as 80% to 100%.

P.title: el-ev.c5.text
Electricity: Most EVs use about 400 V packs. Some newer cars, such as the XPeng G9 and Porsche Taycan, use 800 V platforms, which allow higher charging power with less current and heat.

P.title: el-ev.c6.text
Electricity: Type 2 is the standard AC plug in Europe. CCS2 adds two big DC pins below it for fast charging. Older Japanese cars may use CHAdeMO.

P.title: el-ev.c7.text
Electricity: Smart wallboxes can follow cheaper night tariffs, use surplus solar, and reduce power if the house is near its contracted limit (load balancing), so the main breaker doesn't trip.

P.title: el-ev.c8.text
Electricity: Portugal's public charging network is coordinated by Mobi.E. You can use most public chargers with one card or app from any supplier (CEME), and pay the operator, the supplier and network fees.

P.title: el-ev.c8.viz.steps.0
Electricity: Choose a supplier card or app

P.title: el-ev.c8.viz.steps.1
Electricity: Plug in at any Mobi.E point

P.title: el-ev.c9.text
Electricity: Some energy is lost as heat while charging, typically about 10% for AC home charging, sometimes more at very low power. The meter at the wallbox shows more kWh than the battery receives.

P.title: el-tariffs.summary
Electricity: Bills, tariffs and where the kWh go.

P.title: el-tariffs.q0.q
Electricity: On a bi-horário tariff, when is energy cheaper?

P.title: el-tariffs.q0.o1
Electricity: Off-peak hours, mostly at night and weekends

P.title: el-tariffs.q0.x
Electricity: Vazio hours are the cheap period.

P.title: el-tariffs.q1.q
Electricity: Roughly how much less electricity does an LED use than an incandescent bulb for the same light?

P.title: el-tariffs.q2.q
Electricity: Which is usually one of the largest single loads at home?

P.title: el-tariffs.q2.x
Electricity: Heating water takes a lot of energy.

P.title: el-tariffs.c0.text
Electricity: A Portuguese electricity bill has a fixed part (contracted power, per day), an energy part (per kWh), network access charges, taxes (VAT, the audiovisual contribution) and sometimes discounts.

P.title: el-tariffs.c1.text
Electricity: Simple tariffs charge the same price all day. Two-period (bi-horário) tariffs have cheaper off-peak (vazio) hours, mostly at night and weekends; three-period (tri-horário) splits peak and shoulder hours too.

P.title: el-tariffs.c1.viz.r.items.1
Electricity: worth it if you shift load

P.title: el-tariffs.c2.text
Electricity: It usually pays if you can move a good share of your consumption, often around 40% or more, to off-peak hours: EV charging, water heating, washing machine and dishwasher on a timer.

P.title: el-tariffs.c3.text
Electricity: In a typical home, heating and hot water are the biggest users, followed by cooking, refrigeration, laundry and lighting. An EV can easily double household consumption.

P.title: el-tariffs.c4.text
Electricity: A fridge-freezer cycles on and off 24/7. A modern efficient one uses about 150–250 kWh a year; an old one can use two or three times more.

P.title: el-tariffs.c5.text
Electricity: EU energy labels rate appliances from A (best) to G and show annual consumption in kWh. The scale was rescaled in 2021, so a new "C" can be better than an old "A+++".

P.title: el-tariffs.c6.text
Electricity: LED bulbs use about 80–90% less electricity than old incandescent bulbs for the same light and last much longer. Light output is measured in lumens, not watts.

P.title: el-tariffs.c7.text
Electricity: An electric water heater (termoacumulador) is often one of the biggest single loads. A timer for cheap hours, a lower thermostat setting (around 50–55 °C), and good insulation cut costs. Heat pump water heaters use about a third of the energy.

P.title: el-tariffs.c8.text
Electricity: Smart meters and clamp-based monitors (for example with Home Assistant) show consumption in real time, revealing standby loads and expensive habits.

P.title: el-tariffs.c8.viz.steps.0
Electricity: Clamp sensor on the main cable

P.title: el-tariffs.c9.text
Electricity: In Portugal, neighbours, businesses and municipalities can form renewable energy communities and share solar production through the grid, paying network fees on shared energy.

P.title: el-heat.summary
Electricity: Resistive heat, heat pumps, ovens and hobs.

P.title: el-heat.q0.q
Electricity: A heat pump with a SCOP of 4 using 1,000 kWh delivers about…

P.title: el-heat.q1.q
Electricity: Which hob puts the most energy into the pan?

P.title: el-heat.q2.q
Electricity: Do all resistive electric heaters give the same heat per kWh?

P.title: el-heat.q2.o0
Electricity: Yes, 1 kWh in gives 1 kWh of heat

P.title: el-heat.q2.x
Electricity: They differ in delivery, not efficiency.

P.title: el-heat.c0.text
Electricity: Heaters, kettles, ovens and water heaters turn electricity into heat through resistance: 1 kWh of electricity gives 1 kWh of heat. That's 100% efficient, yet still expensive compared with a heat pump.

P.title: el-heat.c1.text
Electricity: A heat pump moves heat from outside air (or the ground) into the house. Typical seasonal efficiency (SCOP) is 3–4: 1 kWh of electricity delivers 3–4 kWh of heat.

P.title: el-heat.c1.viz.unit
Electricity: kWh of heat per kWh of electricity

P.title: el-heat.c2.text
Electricity: Air-to-air heat pumps are the familiar split air conditioners that also heat. Air-to-water units heat water for radiators, underfloor heating and hot taps.

P.title: el-heat.c3.text
Electricity: All resistive heaters give the same heat per kWh. They differ in how they deliver it: oil-filled radiators are slow and steady, convectors warm air quickly, radiant panels warm people and objects directly.

P.title: el-heat.c4.title
Electricity: Kettles: heat only what you need

P.title: el-heat.c4.text
Electricity: A 2 kW kettle boils 1 litre in about 3 minutes. Boiling a full kettle for one cup wastes energy and time.

P.title: el-heat.c5.text
Electricity: Induction heats the pan directly and is about 85–90% efficient. Ceramic (radiant) hobs are around 70%, gas burners around 40–55%. Induction is also faster and easier to control.

P.title: el-heat.c6.text
Electricity: Heating a large oven cavity takes energy before any cooking starts. Small appliances like air fryers and microwaves heat less volume and often use far less energy for small portions.

P.title: el-heat.c7.text
Electricity: Every degree lower on the thermostat saves roughly 5–10% of heating energy. Timers and smart thermostats heat rooms only when they're used.

P.title: el-heat.c8.text
Electricity: The cheapest kWh is the one you don't need. Roof and wall insulation, better windows and draught sealing reduce heating needs before you upgrade the heater.

P.title: el-heat.c9.text
Electricity: Despite the mild climate, many Portuguese homes are poorly insulated and cold in winter. Portugal has had one of the higher rates of energy poverty in the EU, which is why efficiency programmes subsidise insulation and heat pumps.

P.title: el-static.q0.q
Electricity: Why are you safe inside a car during lightning?

P.title: el-static.q0.o1
Electricity: The metal body conducts the current around you

P.title: el-static.q0.o2
Electricity: Cars are too low to be hit

P.title: el-static.q0.x
Electricity: It acts as a Faraday cage.

P.title: el-static.q1.q
Electricity: Static shocks are more common when…

P.title: el-static.q1.x
Electricity: Dry air lets charge build up.

P.title: el-static.q2.q
Electricity: A typical lightning current is around…

P.title: el-static.q2.x
Electricity: Tens of thousands of amps for microseconds.

P.title: el-static.c0.text
Electricity: Rubbing two materials together transfers electrons from one to the other. One becomes negatively charged, the other positively. The charge stays put ("static") until it finds a path.

P.title: el-static.c1.text
Electricity: Walking on carpet in dry weather builds up charge on your body, sometimes thousands of volts. Touch a metal door handle and it discharges in a tiny spark. Harmless to you, but deadly for electronics.

P.title: el-static.c2.text
Electricity: Electrostatic discharge can destroy chips with voltages too small to feel. That's why boards ship in anti-static bags and technicians wear wrist straps.

P.title: el-static.c3.text
Electricity: Inside storm clouds, ice crystals and soft hail collide in strong updrafts, separating charge. The top of the cloud becomes positive and the bottom negative, until the air breaks down in a giant spark.

P.title: el-static.c4.text
Electricity: A typical lightning bolt carries around 30,000 amps, at hundreds of millions of volts, for a few microseconds, and heats the air to around 30,000 °C, about five times hotter than the Sun's surface.

P.title: el-static.c5.text
Electricity: A lightning rod offers an easy path to earth, so a strike flows safely down a conductor instead of through the building. Benjamin Franklin popularised them in the 1750s.

P.title: el-static.c6.text
Electricity: A metal car body acts as a Faraday cage: current flows around the outside of the metal shell, not through the people inside. It's the metal, not the rubber tyres, that protects you.

P.title: el-static.c6.viz.items.0.r
Electricity: the metal body carries the current around you

P.title: el-static.c7.text
Electricity: If thunder is audible, you're within striking distance. Go indoors or into a car, stay away from tall isolated trees, hilltops and water, and wait 30 minutes after the last thunder.

P.title: el-static.c7.viz.items.3
Electricity: Wait 30 minutes after the last thunder

P.title: el-static.c8.text
Electricity: A nearby strike can induce surges in power and telephone lines that damage electronics. Surge protection devices at the fuse board and on sensitive equipment help.

P.title: el-static.c9.text
Electricity: Flowing fuel, powders and plastic films can build up dangerous static. Fuel stations, grain silos and paint shops use earthing and bonding to prevent sparks that could ignite vapours or dust.

P.title: el-safety.summary
Electricity: Rules that keep people and homes safe.

P.title: el-safety.q0.q
Electricity: What should you do first if someone is stuck to a live appliance?

P.title: el-safety.q0.o1
Electricity: Switch off the power or separate them with something dry and non-conductive

P.title: el-safety.q0.x
Electricity: Never touch them while they're energised.

P.title: el-safety.q1.o1
Electricity: Higher resistance makes them heat up and can start fires

P.title: el-safety.q1.o2
Electricity: They lower the voltage to zero

P.title: el-safety.q1.x
Electricity: Heat and oxidation make them worse.

P.title: el-safety.q2.q
Electricity: Which job should be left to a qualified electrician?

P.title: el-safety.q2.o1
Electricity: Adding a new circuit to the fuse board

P.title: el-safety.q2.x
Electricity: Fixed installation work needs a professional.

P.title: el-safety.c0.text
Electricity: Electricity hurts in three ways: electric shock (current through the body), burns (from arcs or hot surfaces) and fire (from overheating cables or connections).

P.title: el-safety.c1.text
Electricity: Current from hand to hand or hand to foot crosses the chest and heart, the most dangerous paths. Wet skin has much lower resistance, letting more current flow at the same voltage.

P.title: el-safety.c2.text
Electricity: Bathrooms and kitchens have special rules: zones around baths and showers limit which equipment can go where, and all circuits should be protected by a 30 mA RCD.

P.title: el-safety.c2.viz.items.3
Electricity: Never use mains devices in the bath

P.title: el-safety.c3.text
Electricity: A loose screw terminal has a small contact area and higher resistance, so it heats up, oxidises and heats further. Many electrical fires start at a connection, not in the middle of a cable.

P.title: el-safety.c4.text
Electricity: Call an electrician if you see scorch marks, smell burning plastic, hear crackling, feel warm sockets or switches, or if breakers trip repeatedly.

P.title: el-safety.c5.text
Electricity: Don't touch them while they're in contact with the source. Switch off the power or separate them with something dry and non-conductive, call 112, and start CPR if needed.

P.title: el-safety.c6.text
Electricity: Changing a light bulb or plugging in appliances is fine. New circuits, fuse-board work and anything in the fixed installation should be done by a qualified electrician, and in Portugal new installations need certification.

P.title: el-safety.c7.text
Electricity: Plugging several high-power appliances into one multi-way adapter can overload it and the socket behind it. Heaters, kettles and irons should each have their own wall socket.

P.title: el-safety.c7.viz.items.0.r
Electricity: one high-power appliance per wall socket

P.title: el-safety.c8.text
Electricity: Never fly drones or kites, or raise ladders and boat masts, near overhead power lines. High voltage can arc across the air gap without contact.

P.title: el-safety.c8.viz.items.1
Electricity: No kites or drones near lines

P.title: el-safety.c9.text
Electricity: Only 230 V is enough to kill. What matters is the current through the body, and at 230 V a wet hand-to-hand path can easily pass more than the 30–50 mA that can disturb the heart.

P.title: el-backup.summary
Electricity: Storing solar power and keeping the lights on.

P.title: el-backup.q0.q
Electricity: Why do many solar systems switch off during a blackout?

P.title: el-backup.q0.o1
Electricity: To avoid feeding power into lines that workers believe are dead

P.title: el-backup.q1.q
Electricity: How should you size a home battery?

P.title: el-backup.q1.o1
Electricity: Around your evening and night consumption

P.title: el-backup.q1.x
Electricity: Store what you'd otherwise buy after sunset.

P.title: el-backup.q2.q
Electricity: Where must a petrol generator run?

P.title: el-backup.c0.text
Electricity: A battery stores midday solar surplus for the evening, raising self-consumption, and can shift cheap night energy to expensive hours. Some systems also provide backup during outages.

P.title: el-backup.c1.text
Electricity: Size the battery to your evening and night consumption, not your whole day. Many homes use 5–10 kWh between sunset and sunrise.

P.title: el-backup.c2.text
Electricity: A hybrid inverter connects panels, battery, house and grid, deciding where power flows: to the house first, then the battery, then export.

P.title: el-backup.c3.text
Electricity: Many grid-tied solar systems shut down during a blackout for safety, so line workers aren't hurt by power fed back. Backup needs an inverter with an islanding switch and a backup circuit.

P.title: el-backup.c4.text
Electricity: Rather than backing up the whole house, many systems feed an "essential loads" panel: fridge, lights, router, boiler controls, a few sockets.

P.title: el-backup.c5.text
Electricity: An uninterruptible power supply keeps a computer, NAS or network running for minutes during a cut and allows a clean shutdown. It's rated in VA and in runtime at a given load.

P.title: el-backup.c5.viz.steps.1
Electricity: UPS battery takes over in milliseconds

P.title: el-backup.c6.text
Electricity: Portable petrol generators provide backup but must never run indoors (carbon monoxide). Connecting one to the house requires a proper changeover switch so it can't feed the grid.

P.title: el-backup.c6.viz.items.0.r
Electricity: changeover switch installed by an electrician

P.title: el-backup.c6.viz.items.1.r
Electricity: run it outdoors, away from windows

P.title: el-backup.c7.text
Electricity: Some EVs can power a home through bidirectional charging (V2H) or supply appliances via a socket (V2L). An EV battery of 70 kWh could run a typical home for days.

P.title: el-backup.c8.text
Electricity: Home batteries don't always pay for themselves on savings alone. The case improves with large evening consumption, time-of-use tariffs, low feed-in prices, or a strong need for backup.

P.title: el-backup.c8.viz.items.1
Electricity: Big price gap between peak and off-peak

P.title: el-backup.c9.text
Electricity: Install batteries in a ventilated, cool, dry place, away from bedrooms and exits, with clearances as the manufacturer specifies. LFP chemistry is preferred for homes because it's more thermally stable.

P.title: el-history.summary
Electricity: From amber to the smart grid.

P.title: el-history.q0.x
Electricity: Volta built the first battery in 1800.

P.title: el-history.q1.x
Electricity: Faraday showed moving magnets induce current.

P.title: el-history.q2.x
Electricity: Transistors made electronics small and reliable.

P.title: el-history.c0.text
Electricity: Ancient Greeks noticed that rubbed amber attracted feathers. The Greek word for amber, "elektron", gave us "electricity", a term coined by William Gilbert around 1600.

P.title: el-history.c1.text
Electricity: Alessandro Volta stacked discs of zinc and copper separated by brine-soaked cloth: the first battery to give a steady current. The volt is named after him.

P.title: el-history.c2.text
Electricity: In 1831 Michael Faraday showed that moving magnets induce currents, the basis of every generator and transformer. He had little formal education and became one of the greatest experimenters ever.

P.title: el-history.c3.text
Electricity: In the 1860s James Clerk Maxwell wrote four equations unifying electricity, magnetism and light. They predicted radio waves, which Hertz demonstrated in 1887.

P.title: el-history.c4.text
Electricity: Many inventors worked on electric light. In 1879 Edison and, in Britain, Swan produced practical long-lasting carbon-filament bulbs. Edison also built the power stations and network to sell electricity.

P.title: el-history.c4.viz.events.2.l
Electricity: homes widely electrified in the US

P.title: el-history.c5.text
Electricity: The first electric lights in Portugal were switched on in Cascais in 1878. Large hydroelectric dams from the 1950s onward, on rivers such as the Zêzere and the Douro, powered the country's electrification.

P.title: el-history.c6.text
Electricity: At Bell Labs, Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley built the first transistor. It replaced bulky vacuum tubes and made modern electronics, computers and phones possible.

P.title: el-history.c7.text
Electricity: The first nuclear power plants appeared in the 1950s. From the 2000s, wind and then solar grew rapidly as costs fell; solar module prices dropped by around 90% in the 2010s.

P.title: el-history.c8.text
Electricity: Many units honour scientists: volt (Volta), ampere (Ampère), ohm (Ohm), watt (Watt), hertz (Hertz), coulomb (Coulomb), tesla (Tesla).

P.title: el-history.c9.text
Electricity: Electricity is taking over more of energy use: cars, heating, industry. The challenges now are storage, grid expansion, and matching variable renewable supply with demand.
